state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are watching a movie where the main character, Fido, is walking away from his home, then standing still for a while, and finally walking back towards his home. Just like in the graph, the negative-sloping section represents Fido moving away from his home. Let's focus on how we can interpret this movement on the graph to understand Fido's journey better.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it a bit better now. So, the negative slope means Fido is actually moving back towards home instead of just sleeping? But how do I know when he’s moving away or coming back just by looking at the graph?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are on a rollercoaster ride that goes up a hill, levels off for a bit, and then goes back down. Just like Fido's journey on the graph, the negative-sloping section represents him moving back towards home. To know when he's moving away or coming back, focus on the direction of the slope and how it corresponds to Fido's movement.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming negative slope means moving away from home when it actually means returning), fails to address the student's confusion about rest versus movement, and the student shows no improvement in understanding the actual misconception by the end.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (watching a movie of a dog walking, riding a rollercoaster) to help the student understand the abstract concept of interpreting slopes on a distance-time graph, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
